oewn-02506927-v.learner: To put someone on trial, or to sit as the judge at someone's trial.
examples: He was tried for stealing a car and sent to prison.

oewn-00047034-v.learner: To put on a piece of clothing to see whether it fits and looks nice.
examples: She tried the coat on before she bought it.

oewn-02506551-v.learner: To look at the evidence in a case, or to hear a case, in a court of law.
examples: The case was tried in a court far from the town where the crime happened.

oewn-01802793-v.learner: To cause someone pain or trouble.
examples: She was sorely tried by her long illness.

oewn-01802463-v.learner: To test how much something can take before it reaches its limit.
examples: His endless questions tried her patience.

oewn-00445930-v.learner: To melt fat or lard so that the unclean parts can be taken out of it.
examples: They tried the lard in a big pot over the fire.

oewn-02256551-v.learner: To give money, usually in return for things you buy or work someone does.
examples: I paid ten pounds for the book.

oewn-02257739-v.learner: To clear or cancel a debt by giving what you owe.
examples: He owed money for months, but at last he paid up.

oewn-00739889-v.learner: To suffer a cost or a punishment because of something you did.
examples: He will pay for his rudeness one day.

oewn-00734247-v.learner: To give or devote something, such as your attention, to someone or something.
examples: For the whole lesson she paid careful attention to the teacher.

oewn-02258264-v.learner: To do or give something to someone in return for what they did.
examples: They paid the boy for his help with a free meal.

oewn-02349239-v.learner: To make up for something by giving something back.
examples: I can never pay back such a kindness.
It pays to be honest with your friends.

oewn-02296669-v.learner: To bring in an amount, such as money earned.
examples: The savings account pays five per cent a year.

oewn-02126996-s.learner: Serious enough that it must not be treated as small or unimportant.
examples: Loneliness is a real problem for many old people.

oewn-00013681-s.learner: able to be treated as a fact.
examples: The new law brought few real benefits to the poor.

oewn-00628097-a.learner: Having substance, or able to be treated as a fact; not imagined.
examples: It was only a dream; none of it was real.

oewn-01948221-s.learner: Matching what is really there or really true.
examples: The painter gave a real picture of the harbour, true in every detail.

oewn-01946213-a.learner: Describing an amount of money that has been changed to allow for prices rising over time.
examples: Real wages fell last year, even though people were paid more.

oewn-02400973-s.learner: Of property: fixed in one place and not able to be moved.
examples: Houses and land are real property.

oewn-08404661-n.learner: the small group of fashionable people at the top of social life.
examples: She was the most admired young woman in London society that season.

oewn-14468845-n.learner: The state of being relaxed and not feeling any pain.
examples: After the long walk, he sat by the fire in comfort.

oewn-14515473-n.learner: Freedom from money troubles, which lets you live comfortably.
examples: They lived in comfort on the money his father had left.

oewn-04040471-n.learner: A bed cover made of two layers of cloth with soft filling, sewn together.
examples: She pulled the comfort up to her chin.

oewn-01213675-n.learner: Help, such as help given to an enemy or to a known criminal.
examples: The town was accused of giving comfort to the enemy.

oewn-00601387-v.learner: To be a student of a subject.
examples: She is learning French at school.

oewn-00605971-v.learner: To put something into your memory; to learn it by heart.
examples: The children had to learn the poem by Friday.

oewn-00830768-v.learner: To teach someone skills or knowledge.
examples: I'll learn you to play the fiddle if you like.

oewn-05838383-n.learner: Someone or something that causes you trouble or makes you unhappy.
examples: Her little brother can be a real pain.

connotation.why: labels a person or thing a nuisance rather than a problem

oewn-01215372-n.learner: Loyal support for a cause, a political party or a religion.
examples: Nothing could shake his attachment to the cause of reform.

oewn-00380230-n.learner: The act of fixing or joining one thing onto something else.
examples: The attachment of a label to each box took an hour.

oewn-00148415-n.learner: The act of fastening things together.
examples: The attachment of the two boards needed only a few nails.

oewn-06566972-n.learner: A written court order that allows property to be taken, because it may be needed to pay what a court decides is owed.
examples: The bank got an attachment on his house to cover the debt.

oewn-05936599-n.learner: A picture of the world held in the mind, made of ideas and actions, which can change when you learn new things.
examples: The child's scheme of how animals behave changed after she saw the fox.

oewn-06769391-n.learner: Something said to avoid answering a question, using cleverness or tricks.
examples: His reply was a clever scheme to dodge the question.

connotation.why: casts an answer as a trick rather than a reply

oewn-11474277-n.learner: Something that happens at one single point in space and time; the basic thing observed in relativity theory.
examples: In relativity, each event has its own place and time.
